passages.t: Jotham, a steady king, and a corrupt people
passages.happening: Jotham becomes king at twenty-five and reigns sixteen years (verse 1). ‘And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father Uzziah had done. In addition, he did not enter the temple of the LORD. But the people still behaved corruptly’ (verse 2). He builds the Upper Gate of the temple, works on the wall of Ophel, and builds cities, fortresses and towers (verses 3-4). He defeats the Ammonites, and they pay tribute for three years (verse 5). ‘So Jotham grew powerful because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God’ (verse 6). He dies and is buried in the City of David, and Ahaz his son reigns (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
After three kings who started well and ended badly, Jotham is a quiet relief: no late fall. His short chapter is the calm between Uzziah's disgrace and the disaster of Ahaz. The one warning is in verse 2: the people still behaved corruptly, shachat, the verb used in Genesis of the earth before the flood. A faithful king can build walls and win wars, but he cannot by himself turn a nation's heart.

Jotham governed first as regent while his father lived apart, then as king; a common reconstruction places his rule about 750 to 735 BC, with the sixteen years overlapping his father's last years. Second Kings 15 adds that in his days the LORD began to send Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel against Judah, the threat that would break out under Ahaz. Isaiah, Hosea and Micah all name Jotham among the kings in whose days they spoke, and their words show the corruption Chronicles only mentions: injustice in the courts, greed for land, worship without obedience. Assyria was rising again under Tiglath-pileser the Third, who took the throne around 745 BC.

The Upper Gate and the wall of Ophel, the ridge between the old City of David and the temple mount, strengthened Jerusalem. The Ammonite tribute came in silver and grain; a cor was a large dry measure, perhaps a couple of hundred liters, and that the payments lasted only three years hints that Ammon's submission did not last. Verse 6 gives the chapter's theology in one picture: he ordered, kun, his ways, derekh, his road, before God.
passages.later: Micah's book opens, ‘This is the word of the LORD that came to Micah the Moreshite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah’ (Micah 1:1).
passages.hard:
Jotham reigned sixteen years here, but 2 Kings 15:30 mentions his twentieth year. How do these fit?

The kings of Israel and Judah were dated by counting systems that sometimes overlapped. Jotham began governing while his father was still alive, and his son Ahaz may also have begun ruling before Jotham died. Many historians, following reconstructions such as Edwin Thiele's, explain the twentieth year as counting from the start of Jotham's regency to a date after Ahaz had effectively taken over, while the sixteen years count his reign in a narrower sense. Others think the numbers reflect different sources or later scribal adjustments. The difference is real, but it comes from the complexity of ancient dating, not from a contradiction about who ruled.
passages.asks: Jotham ordered his ways before God, and the people around him still went their own way. Ask whether you can be faithful without being able to make others so. And ask what it would mean to order your ways before God this week, one road at a time.
